claims.text: Near-simultaneous activation of all metal precursors promotes formation of homogeneous high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Kinetically synchronized reduction prevents individual elements from nucleating separately.
Preventing separate nucleation suppresses phase segregation.
The proposed starting material is a uniformly blended, single-phase mixture of noble- and non-noble-metal salts or complexes.
A rapid-onset thermal or chemical trigger can minimize differences in activation timing among the constituent elements.
Synchronized activation produces nanoscale nuclei containing uniformly incorporated atoms from all constituent elements.
Uniform multielement incorporation in the nuclei results in high surface-atom exposure across the multimetal system.
Concurrent deposition kinetically traps the constituent elements in a metastable single-phase alloy.
Staggered activation promotes early elemental segregation or overgrowth.
Early elemental segregation or overgrowth leads to phase separation or uncontrolled nanoparticle morphology.
Synchronized activation will yield nanoparticles with more uniform elemental distributions than the asynchronous baseline.
Synchronized activation will yield greater phase purity and more consistent morphology than the asynchronous baseline.
Differences in reduction or nucleation timing cause preferential elemental segregation and inhomogeneous morphology under baseline processing.
Asynchronous activation is associated with higher decomposition temperatures.
The proposed mechanism applies principally when constituent precursors have relatively comparable activation energies and reduction potentials.
The mechanism may fail when constituent precursors have inherently disparate activation kinetics.
The mechanism may fail when post-synthesis diffusion dominates structural evolution.
Precursor chemistry and support interactions may also influence the outcome.
